meta.scope_note: A comparative selection of European monarchies and predecessor realms, including all surviving sovereign monarchies at the 2026 snapshot. Coverage is selective; records distinguish annual overlap from simultaneous rule. Claim-level sourcing and regional review remain in progress.

polities.name: Roman Empire
polities.summary: The Roman imperial state from the Augustan settlement to 395, when separate eastern and western courts became enduring. Romans did not regard this administrative division as the creation of two unrelated empires.

polities.name: Western Roman Empire
polities.summary: The western imperial court after the division of 395, ending conventionally in 476.

polities.name: Eastern Roman / Byzantine Empire
polities.summary: The eastern Roman imperial tradition centred on Constantinople; modern scholarship conventionally calls its medieval phase Byzantine. After the crusader capture of 1204, rival successor states claimed the Roman inheritance until the Nicaean regime recovered Constantinople in 1261.

polities.name: Frankish Realm (Francia)
polities.summary: Francia is the historical name used here for the Merovingian and Carolingian Frankish realm. It ends with the 843 partition that created West, Middle and East Francia.

polities.name: Holy Roman Empire
polities.summary: A composite elective empire in Central Europe. This project begins the continuous imperial phase with Otto I in 962 and treats Charlemagne's coronation as a precursor event.

polities.name: French Monarchy
polities.summary: This lane begins with West Francia after the partition of the wider Frankish realm in 843, then follows the Kingdom of France and the Bourbon and July restorations.

polities.name: Kingdom of England
polities.summary: The English kingdom from Æthelstan, interrupted by the republican Interregnum of 1649–1660, until the Acts of Union created Great Britain in 1707.

polities.name: Kingdom of Scotland
polities.summary: The Scottish royal line is shown from the traditional accession of Cináed mac Ailpín in 843, although he was king of the Picts and the kingdom of Alba emerged gradually. Monarchical government was interrupted by Cromwellian conquest before the 1660 Restoration.

polities.name: Kingdom of Great Britain
polities.summary: The state created by the union of England and Scotland, lasting until union with Ireland in 1801.

polities.name: United Kingdom
polities.summary: The constitutional monarchy created in 1801 and continued after most of Ireland left the union.

polities.name: Crown of Castile
polities.summary: The composite Crown of Castile, joined dynastically with Aragon and later integrated into the Spanish monarchy.

polities.name: Crown of Aragon
polities.summary: A composite Mediterranean monarchy joined dynastically with Castile in the late fifteenth century.

polities.name: Kingdom of Navarre
polities.summary: A Pyrenean kingdom divided between Spain and France; the northern kingdom was incorporated into France in 1620.

polities.name: Kingdom of Portugal
polities.summary: The Portuguese monarchy from its twelfth-century independence to the republic of 1910.

polities.name: Spain
polities.summary: The Spanish monarchy, shown first as the dynastic union of Castile and Aragon and later under more centralized institutions. The First and Second Republics are explicit interruptions; the Bonaparte monarchy and the revolutionary succession of 1868–1874 are separately qualified.

polities.name: Denmark
polities.summary: One of Europe's oldest continuing monarchies, central to the Kalmar Union and the composite monarchy of Denmark–Norway.

polities.name: Norway
polities.summary: The Norwegian royal line is conventionally traced to Harald Fairhair, but his chronology and the extent of his power are uncertain; durable political unification belongs to the eleventh century. Norway later spent long periods in unions with Denmark and Sweden.

polities.name: Sweden
polities.summary: The Swedish monarchy is shown from the first ruler in the Royal Court's conventional list, Erik Segersäll around 970, through medieval elective kingship, the Vasa hereditary monarchy and the Bernadotte dynasty.

polities.name: Polish Monarchy and Kingdom
polities.summary: The Polish monarchy from the first coronation in 1025. Royal coronations and effective unity lapsed for long periods before the kingdom was durably reunited in 1320; Poland was later joined first personally and then constitutionally with Lithuania.

polities.name: Grand Duchy of Lithuania
polities.summary: A major eastern European grand duchy joined with Poland under the Jagiellons and the Union of Lublin.

polities.name: Kyivan Rus’
polities.summary: A medieval polity centred on Kyiv and ruled by branches of the Rurik dynasty. It is shown as shared eastern European history, not as the exclusive predecessor of any one modern nation.

polities.name: Galicia–Volhynia / Kingdom of Ruthenia
polities.summary: A western Rus’ principality founded by the union of Galicia and Volhynia in 1199; Danylo was crowned king in 1253, and the polity ended after its last prince died in 1340.

polities.name: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
polities.summary: A federative elective monarchy created by the Union of Lublin and ended by the partitions of Poland.

polities.name: Kingdom of Bohemia
polities.summary: A kingdom of the Bohemian Crown within the Holy Roman Empire and later the Habsburg monarchy.

polities.name: Kingdom of Hungary
polities.summary: The Hungarian crown from Stephen I through the partition after Mohács and Habsburg rule; the regency of 1920–1946 retained the name kingdom without a king.

polities.name: Archduchy and Empire of Austria
polities.summary: The Habsburg hereditary lands and Austrian Empire before the dual monarchy of 1867.

polities.name: Austria-Hungary
polities.summary: The Dual Monarchy created by the Austro-Hungarian Compromise and dissolved in 1918.

polities.name: Principality and Grand Principality of Moscow
polities.summary: The Rurikid principality centred on Moscow that expanded into the core of the Russian state. Its start is conventional because historians differ over when Muscovy became a distinct polity.

polities.name: Tsardom and Empire of Russia
polities.summary: The Russian monarchy from Ivan IV's coronation as tsar to the revolutions of 1917.

polities.name: Kingdom of Prussia
polities.summary: The Hohenzollern kingdom that led German unification and became the largest constituent state of the German Empire.

polities.name: German Empire
polities.summary: The federal German monarchy proclaimed in 1871 under the Prussian Hohenzollerns.

polities.name: Kingdom of the Netherlands
polities.summary: The constitutional monarchy created after the Napoleonic Wars under Orange-Nassau.

polities.name: Belgium
polities.summary: The constitutional monarchy established after the Belgian Revolution.

polities.name: Savoy and the Kingdom of Sardinia
polities.summary: The Savoyard monarchy that became the Kingdom of Sardinia and led Italian unification.

polities.name: Kingdom of Italy
polities.summary: The Savoy monarchy of united Italy, ended by referendum after the Second World War.

polities.name: Kingdom of the Two Sicilies
polities.summary: The separate crowns of Naples and island Sicily were formally united in 1816. Bourbon rule ended during Italian unification in 1860–1861.

polities.name: Serbian Kingdoms
polities.summary: The medieval Serbian kingdom, empire and despotate, followed by the modern Kingdom of Serbia, one of the states whose union produced the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes in 1918.

polities.name: Kingdom of Yugoslavia
polities.summary: The South Slav monarchy formed in 1918 and abolished after the Second World War.

polities.name: Bulgarian Empires and Kingdom
polities.summary: The medieval Bulgarian empires and the modern kingdom abolished in 1946.

polities.name: Kingdom of Romania
polities.summary: The Romanian monarchy under Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, ended in 1947.

polities.name: Kingdom of Greece
polities.summary: The modern Greek monarchy, interrupted in 1924 and finally abolished in 1973–1974.

polities.name: Ottoman Empire
polities.summary: A transcontinental sultanate included because its European territories and diplomacy were central to European monarchical history.

polities.name: Croatian Kingdom and Crown
polities.summary: The medieval Croatian crown continued under shared Hungarian and then Habsburg monarchs. Later constitutional arrangements included the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia from 1868 to 1918; the changing territorial scope is represented by separate phases.

polities.name: Grand Duchy of Luxembourg
polities.summary: The world's only surviving sovereign grand duchy.

polities.name: Principality of Monaco
polities.summary: The Grimaldi principality, interrupted by French annexation from 1793 to 1814, and now one of Europe's surviving hereditary monarchies.

polities.name: Principality of Liechtenstein
polities.summary: An Alpine principality created in 1719, sovereign since 1806 and ruled by the House of Liechtenstein.

polities.name: Co-Principality of Andorra
polities.summary: A parliamentary co-principality whose joint heads are the Bishop of Urgell and the French head of state.

polities.name: Papal States and Vatican City
polities.summary: Papal temporal rule in central Italy was interrupted during the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic eras and ended in 1870; the Lateran Treaty created Vatican City and restored territorial sovereignty to the pope in 1929.

polities.name: Kingdom of Ireland
polities.summary: Ireland became a kingdom under Henry VIII in 1542. Its crown was shared with England and later Great Britain; the monarchy was interrupted during the Commonwealth. The 1801 union incorporated Ireland and Great Britain into the United Kingdom.

polities.name: East Francia and the German kingdom
polities.summary: The eastern Frankish kingdom created at Verdun. The lane follows the royal line to Otto I’s imperial coronation in 962; the German kingship continued within the empire after this editorial boundary.

polities.name: Middle Francia
polities.summary: Lothair I’s middle kingdom stretched from the North Sea to Italy. His sons divided it in 855 into Lotharingia, Italy and Provence. Those successor kingdoms are outside this edition.

polities.name: Kingdom of Sicily
polities.summary: Founded in 1130, the Norman kingdom initially included the southern mainland. After 1282 this lane follows the island crown, which retained its own succession and institutions until union with Naples in 1816.

polities.name: Kingdom of Naples
polities.summary: The mainland crown separated from island Sicily after the Sicilian Vespers in 1282. Naples had its own rulers, including French rulers while the Bourbons remained in Sicily, before the two crowns united in 1816.

phases.name: Roman imperial state before the enduring court division
phases.note: The start date follows Augustus' constitutional settlement of 27 BCE. The 395 endpoint is an editorial boundary between lanes: contemporaries continued to conceive a single Roman Empire governed by more than one court.

relationships.label: Iberian Union
relationships.description: The Spanish Habsburgs ruled Portugal in personal union until the Portuguese Restoration.

citations.locator: Introduction and treaty: Habsburg rule 1580–1640, restoration on 1 December 1640, and Spanish recognition in 1668.

relationships.label: Portuguese Restoration
relationships.description: The acclaim of John IV in 1640 ended Habsburg rule over Portugal and began the Braganza dynasty. Portugal had retained a distinct crown during the Iberian Union; Spain recognized the new settlement in 1668.

citations.locator: Introduction and treaty: Habsburg rule 1580–1640, restoration on 1 December 1640, and Spanish recognition in 1668.

relationships.label: Kalmar Union
relationships.description: Denmark, Norway and Sweden remained distinct kingdoms under a common monarch, but Sweden repeatedly rejected or displaced union kings; the 1397–1523 span should not be read as uninterrupted effective government in all three realms.

citations.locator: Erik’s coronation in 1397, Swedish interruptions after 1434, and final separation with Gustav Vasa in 1523. This record denotes the framework, not continuous shared reigns.

relationships.label: Denmark–Norway
relationships.description: After the Reformation settlement of 1536–1537, the Danish monarch governed Denmark and Norway as an unequal composite monarchy with common central direction but distinct laws and territorial identities. It was more than a merely personal union and less than a unitary nation-state.

relationships.label: Sweden–Norway
relationships.description: Norway retained its constitution and institutions while sharing a monarch with Sweden.

citations.locator: Introduction: union with Sweden from 1814 to 1905, with a Norwegian constitution and separate state institutions.

relationships.label: Western Rus’ successor centre
relationships.description: Galicia–Volhynia emerged from principalities formed during the fragmentation of Kyivan Rus’ and became a major western Rus’ centre. The connector records one line of political and cultural continuity, not an exclusive succession to all of Rus’.

relationships.label: Galicia–Volhynia succession
relationships.description: After Yurii II Boleslav died in 1340, Poland and Lithuania contested the inheritance. Galicia passed under Polish rule, while much of Volhynia became part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania through a prolonged struggle rather than a single clean partition.

relationships.label: Polish–Lithuanian dynastic union
relationships.description: The marriage of Jadwiga and Jogaila began a dynastic framework linking Poland and Lithuania in 1386. Grand ducal government and succession remained distinct, and shared personal rule was intermittent before the Union of Lublin in 1569.

citations.locator: History, personal union, real union, and partition sections: 1386 marriage, 1 July 1569 Lublin settlement, and third partition in 1795.

relationships.label: Union of Lublin
relationships.description: The Union of Lublin created a federative Commonwealth with an elected joint monarch.

citations.locator: History, personal union, real union, and partition sections: 1386 marriage, 1 July 1569 Lublin settlement, and third partition in 1795.

relationships.label: Partitions of the Commonwealth
relationships.description: The third partition ended the Commonwealth and divided its remaining territory among Russia, Prussia and Austria.

citations.locator: History, personal union, real union, and partition sections: 1386 marriage, 1 July 1569 Lublin settlement, and third partition in 1795.

relationships.label: Ivan IV crowned tsar
relationships.description: Ivan IV's coronation as tsar in 1547 marks the editorial transition from the Grand Principality of Moscow to the Tsardom of Russia. It was a change of title and political claim under the same Rurikid ruler, not a replacement state.

relationships.label: Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire
relationships.description: Francis II abdicated the imperial crown during the Napoleonic reorganization of Germany. Austria and Prussia became the leading German monarchies but were not direct constitutional successors.

citations.locator: Dissolution in 1806; Austria and Prussia were leading powers rather than constitutional successors.

relationships.label: Austro-Hungarian Compromise
relationships.description: The Habsburg monarchy became a dual state with Austrian and Hungarian governments under one sovereign.

citations.locator: The 1867 Compromise and the Austrian and Hungarian halves of the monarchy.

relationships.label: Prussian king holds the German imperial office
relationships.description: The Prussian king also held the imperial office in the German federation from 1871. This edge identifies the shared ruler; other federal states and the full process of unification are outside this connection.

citations.locator: Overview: German Empire founded under the Prussian king in 1871; monarchy ended in the November Revolution of 1918.

relationships.label: Sardinian monarchy becomes Kingdom of Italy
relationships.description: In March 1861 Victor Emmanuel II assumed the title King of Italy as the Savoyard monarchy and its institutions continued on a larger territorial basis. The preceding annexations are separate events; Venetia followed in 1866 and Rome in 1870.

citations.locator: Founding law, 17 March 1861: Victor Emmanuel II assumes the title King of Italy following annexations to the Sardinian monarchy.

relationships.label: Croatian–Hungarian union
relationships.description: Coloman was crowned king of Croatia in 1102, joining the Croatian and Hungarian crowns. Historians dispute the conquest-versus-agreement framing and the later text of the Pacta conventa is not an authentic document from 1102; Croatia nevertheless retained distinct institutions under the shared crown.

relationships.label: Serbian dynasty in the South Slav kingdom
relationships.description: The Karađorđević dynasty continued from Serbia into the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes in 1918. This edge traces that ruling dynasty. The state also included Montenegro and the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, which are outside the selected lanes; it was renamed Yugoslavia in 1929.

citations.locator: Formation of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes in December 1918 under the Serbian dynasty.

relationships.label: Byzantine conquest of Bulgaria
relationships.description: Basil II completed the conquest of the First Bulgarian Empire.

citations.locator: Medieval history: Byzantine conquest in 1018, Asen revolt in 1185–1186 and Ottoman conquest in 1396. Modern history: republic in 1946. The medieval end date remains disputed in the linked regnal literature.

relationships.label: Second Bulgarian Empire
relationships.description: The Asen uprising restored an independent Bulgarian monarchy.

citations.locator: Medieval history: Byzantine conquest in 1018, Asen revolt in 1185–1186 and Ottoman conquest in 1396. Modern history: republic in 1946. The medieval end date remains disputed in the linked regnal literature.

relationships.label: Ottoman conquest of Bulgaria
relationships.description: The capture of Vidin in 1396 is the conventional endpoint used here for the medieval Bulgarian state. Constantine II’s later position and the extent of continuing independence are disputed; some chronologies extend to 1422.

citations.locator: Medieval history: Byzantine conquest in 1018, Asen revolt in 1185–1186 and Ottoman conquest in 1396. Modern history: republic in 1946. The medieval end date remains disputed in the linked regnal literature.

relationships.label: Ottoman conquest of Serbia
relationships.description: The fall of Smederevo ended the medieval Serbian Despotate.

citations.locator: Medieval history: Ottoman conquest of Smederevo in 1459 ended the medieval Serbian state.

relationships.label: Bourbon Restoration
relationships.description: The Bourbon monarchy returned after Napoleon's defeat, with a brief interruption during the Hundred Days.

citations.locator: Bourbon Restoration 1814–1830; Louis XVIII’s return to Paris on 3 May 1814.

relationships.label: Restoration of the Spanish monarchy
relationships.description: Juan Carlos I became king after Francisco Franco's death and presided over the transition to constitutional democracy.

citations.locator: Constitutional history: monarchy restored in 1975 and transition to the 1978 constitution.

relationships.label: Restoration of the Greek monarchy
relationships.description: A controlled plebiscite restored George II after the Second Hellenic Republic.

citations.locator: Interwar period: restoration of the monarchy in November 1935; the plebiscite’s conditions are discussed in the linked restoration article.

relationships.label: Lateran Treaty
relationships.description: The Lateran Treaty created Vatican City and restored territorial sovereignty to the pope after the loss of the Papal States.

relationships.label: Russian Revolution
relationships.description: Nicholas II abdicated during the February Revolution, ending the Romanov monarchy.

citations.locator: Reign ended with abdication in March 1917 during the February Revolution (Old Style calendar).

relationships.label: End of the Central European empires
relationships.description: Defeat and revolution ended the German and Austro-Hungarian monarchies.

citations.locator: Overview: German Empire founded under the Prussian king in 1871; monarchy ended in the November Revolution of 1918.
October–November 1918 disintegration and Karl’s renunciation of participation in government on 11 November, without a formal abdication.

relationships.label: Abolition of the Ottoman sultanate
relationships.description: The Turkish Grand National Assembly abolished the sultanate.

citations.locator: Grand National Assembly abolished the sultanate on 1 November 1922; republic followed in 1923.

relationships.label: Italian republic
relationships.description: A referendum ended the Savoy monarchy and established the Italian Republic.

citations.locator: Institutional referendum of 2 June 1946 and the end of the Savoy monarchy.

relationships.label: End of the Balkan monarchies
relationships.description: The communist-led constituent assembly abolished Yugoslavia's monarchy in 1945; Bulgaria became a republic after a 1946 referendum held under communist rule; Romania's King Michael was forced to abdicate in 1947.

citations.locator: Medieval history: Byzantine conquest in 1018, Asen revolt in 1185–1186 and Ottoman conquest in 1396. Modern history: republic in 1946. The medieval end date remains disputed in the linked regnal literature.
Postwar history: King Michael was forced to abdicate in December 1947 and a republic was proclaimed.
Kingdom from 1918, royal government in exile 1941–1945, and republic from 1945.

relationships.label: Otto I’s imperial coronation
relationships.description: Otto I, king of the East Franks, was crowned emperor in 962. This marks the chart’s transition to the imperial lane; the German kingship continued within the empire.

relationships.label: Conquest and annexation of the Two Sicilies
relationships.description: Garibaldi’s campaign and Piedmontese intervention overthrew Bourbon rule. Plebiscites accompanied annexation to the Savoyard state in 1860; the Bourbon fortress at Gaeta fell in 1861.

relationships.label: Shared crowns restored
relationships.description: The Restoration returned the English, Scottish and Irish crowns to Charles II in 1660. England and Scotland united as Great Britain in 1707; Ireland remained a separate kingdom.

relationships.label: Union of Naples and Sicily
relationships.description: Ferdinand combined the separate kingdoms of Naples and island Sicily into the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in December 1816.

events.label: Augustan settlement
events.description: Octavian received the title Augustus, conventionally beginning the Roman Principate.

citations.locator: The senate’s grant of the title Augustus in 27 BCE and the beginning of the Principate.

events.label: Enduring division between imperial courts
events.description: Separate western and eastern courts followed the death of Theodosius I. Romans still understood them as parts of one Roman Empire.

citations.locator: Theodosius I and succession in 395: Honorius in the west and Arcadius in the east.

events.label: Western emperor deposed
events.description: Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus.

citations.locator: Chronology: reign 475–476; deposition by Odoacer in 476.

events.label: Charlemagne crowned emperor
events.description: Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne in Rome, reviving an imperial title in western Europe.

citations.locator: Coronation by Pope Leo III in Rome on Christmas Day 800.

events.label: Treaty of Verdun
events.description: The Carolingian realm was divided into western, middle and eastern kingdoms.

citations.locator: Treaty of Verdun, 843: partition between Lothair, Louis and Charles.

events.label: Otto I crowned emperor
events.description: Otto I's coronation begins the continuous imperial line used for the Holy Roman Empire lane.

citations.locator: Origins: Otto I crowned emperor by John XII in 962.

events.label: Norman Conquest
events.description: William of Normandy conquered England and replaced the ruling house.

citations.locator: William’s conquest, Battle of Hastings and accession in 1066.

events.label: Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople
events.description: Crusaders captured Constantinople; Byzantine successor states restored the empire in 1261.

citations.locator: Historical overview: Roman continuity, Constantinople taken in 1204, recovered in 1261, and conquered by the Ottomans in 1453.

events.label: Fall of Constantinople
events.description: The Ottoman capture ended the Eastern Roman Empire.

citations.locator: Historical overview: Roman continuity, Constantinople taken in 1204, recovered in 1261, and conquered by the Ottomans in 1453.

events.label: Castile and Aragon share monarchs
events.description: Ferdinand succeeded in Aragon while Isabella already ruled Castile.

citations.locator: Isabella’s accession in 1474; Ferdinand’s succession to John II in Aragon in 1479 and reciprocal governing powers.

events.label: Charles V elected King of the Romans
events.description: Charles, already joint ruler of the Spanish crowns, was elected King of the Romans in 1519 and crowned emperor by the pope in 1530.

events.label: Union of Lublin
events.description: Poland and Lithuania formed the Commonwealth.

citations.locator: History, personal union, real union, and partition sections: 1386 marriage, 1 July 1569 Lublin settlement, and third partition in 1795.

events.label: Union of the Crowns
events.description: James VI of Scotland inherited England as James I.

citations.locator: James VI’s succession in 1603 and the continued separation of the kingdoms.

events.label: Peace of Westphalia
events.description: The treaties ended the Thirty Years' War and confirmed extensive constitutional rights of the imperial estates. They did not invent the modern sovereign state in a single settlement.

events.label: Acts of Union
events.description: England and Scotland became Great Britain.

citations.locator: Articles of Union: England and Scotland united into Great Britain in 1707.

events.label: Final Nueva Planta decree
events.description: The last of the principal Nueva Planta decrees completed a 1707–1716 reorganization that abolished most separate public institutions of the Crown of Aragon.

events.label: French monarchy abolished
events.description: The National Convention proclaimed the French Republic.

citations.locator: Convention: abolition of monarchy in September 1792 and the beginning of the Republic.

events.label: Holy Roman Empire dissolved
events.description: Francis II laid down the imperial crown during the Napoleonic Wars.

citations.locator: End of the Empire: Francis II relinquished the imperial crown in 1806.

events.label: Congress of Vienna settlement
events.description: The post-Napoleonic settlement restored and created monarchies across Europe.

citations.locator: 1814–1815 negotiations, territorial restoration and the European settlement after Napoleon.

events.label: Revolutions of 1848
events.description: Revolutions challenged monarchies across France, the German states, Italy and the Habsburg lands.

citations.locator: European revolutionary wave beginning in France and spreading to the German states, Habsburg monarchy and Italy.

events.label: Kingdom of Italy proclaimed
events.description: Parliament proclaimed Victor Emmanuel II king of Italy after the incorporation of most of the peninsula; Venetia and Rome were added later.

citations.locator: Founding law, 17 March 1861: Victor Emmanuel II assumes the title King of Italy following annexations to the Sardinian monarchy.

events.label: German Empire proclaimed
events.description: William I of Prussia became German emperor.

citations.locator: Overview: German Empire founded under the Prussian king in 1871; monarchy ended in the November Revolution of 1918.

events.label: Russian monarchy falls
events.description: Nicholas II abdicated amid revolution.

citations.locator: Reign ended with abdication in March 1917 during the February Revolution (Old Style calendar).

events.label: Central European imperial monarchies collapse
events.description: Defeat and revolution ended the German and Austro-Hungarian monarchies in 1918. The wider sequence of imperial collapse ran from Russia in 1917 to abolition of the Ottoman sultanate in 1922.

citations.locator: Overview: German Empire founded under the Prussian king in 1871; monarchy ended in the November Revolution of 1918.

events.label: Postwar monarchical abolitions
events.description: Italy and Bulgaria became republics in 1946, between Yugoslavia's abolition of the monarchy in 1945 and Romania's forced abdication in 1947.

citations.locator: Institutional referendum of 2 June 1946 and the end of the Savoy monarchy.

Kingdom from 1918, royal government in exile 1941–1945, and republic from 1945.

events.label: Spanish monarchy restored
events.description: Juan Carlos I was proclaimed king two days after Franco's death and became head of state under the succession arrangements of the dictatorship; the subsequent transition established a parliamentary monarchy.

events.label: Frederik X succeeds Margrethe II
events.description: Margrethe II abdicated on 14 January and Frederik X acceded as king of Denmark.

events.label: Transitions in Luxembourg, Andorra and Vatican City
events.description: Guillaume became Grand Duke of Luxembourg on 3 October, Josep-Lluís Serrano Pentinat took the oath as Episcopal Co-Prince of Andorra on 26 June, and Leo XIV was elected pope and sovereign of Vatican City on 8 May.

events.label: Haakon VIII succeeds Harald V
events.description: Harald V died on 28 August 2026. His son acceded as Haakon VIII under the Norwegian constitution.

presets.title: The Carolingian partition
presets.description: The Treaty of Verdun divided the Carolingian Empire into western, middle and eastern realms. Those realms shaped later political development but were not modern France, Germany and Italy in embryo.

presets.title: A conqueror in England
presets.description: The Norman Conquest changed the English ruling house and tied the kingdom more tightly to continental politics.

presets.title: The crowns of Charles V
presets.description: Charles's election as King of the Romans added the imperial office to a collection of inherited crowns and lordships across Iberia, Central Europe, Italy and the Low Countries; it did not merge them into one state.

presets.title: A kingdom of Great Britain
presets.description: A century after the Union of the Crowns, England and Scotland became one state while Iberian and Nordic composite monarchies were also changing.

presets.title: Europe after Napoleon
presets.description: The Congress of Vienna restored and rearranged monarchies while recognizing new kingdoms and dynastic settlements.

presets.title: Imperial collapse, 1917–1922
presets.description: The German and Austro-Hungarian monarchies ended in 1918, between the fall of the Russian monarchy in 1917 and abolition of the Ottoman sultanate in 1922.

presets.title: Surviving monarchies · 2026 snapshot
presets.description: Twelve sovereign European states retain monarchical heads of state, ranging from kingdoms to a grand duchy, principalities and an elective papacy.
